22.0.s.en: (1) Ahab allies himself with Jehoshaphat to recover Ramoth-gilead

22.0.0.en: Because of Ahab's humbling himself and his repentance before God, God caused Ben-hadad king of Aram and all the countries surrounding Israel not to fight it, so it lived in peace for three years.

22.0.1.en: Be sure that the shortest way to God's heart is humility and repentance, and you will receive His mercies and tenderness. This humility is not only before God in prayer but is confirmed before others, so that you bear with them and are distinguished by fellowship with God and His love.

22.1.0.en: Jehoshaphat had become related by marriage to Ahab, in that he took Athaliah, Ahab's daughter, as wife for his son Jehoram (2 Chr 18:1, 2), and this was a spiritual concession, because Jehoshaphat worshiped God in His temple in Jerusalem, while Ahab and his family worshiped idols. So Jehoshaphat, who lived in Jerusalem, built on the mountains, went down to Samaria, which is lower than it geographically by about three hundred meters, and at the same time it was a spiritual descent, as we mentioned. He visited Ahab either to show affection, since they were relatives, or perhaps for political and military purposes, for Aram had taken Ramoth-gilead, which is near Jerusalem, at a distance of forty miles, and so represented a danger to the kingdom of Judah, as it could also threaten the kingdom of Israel. Also the kingdom of Assyria had begun to grow strong and could represent a danger to the two kingdoms of Israel and Judah, so the alliance of the two kingdoms, Judah and Israel, is logically useful but spiritually a mistake, because the One who protects Jerusalem is God, who is able to defend it against any human power, as will appear in the days of King Hezekiah (Isa 36, 37).

22.2.0.en: Ramoth-gilead: a city of the Amorites (Deut 4:43), meaning the heights of Gilead. The children of Israel took it and it was given to the tribe of Gad, then it was assigned to the Levites and was one of the cities of refuge. It lies east of the Jordan at a distance of twenty-five miles.

22.2.1.en: Ahab gathered with his servants and counselors and said to them: Ben-hadad king of Aram promised me, when I defeated him, to restore to me the cities which his father Ben-hadad had taken from the children of Israel (ch. 20:34). Since three years have passed and he has not fulfilled his promise, it is certain that he has gone back on it. So Ramoth is our right, and we are negligent in recovering it. Ahab may have been slack in demanding these cities because he was occupied with resisting Assyria, allied with Aram and the Hittites.

22.3.0.en: After Ahab honored Jehoshaphat greatly (2 Chr 18:2), he seduced him and encouraged him to ally with him by fighting Aram, so that they could recover Ramoth-gilead from it. Ahab may have pressed Jehoshaphat and shown him the danger of not recovering it, because it is near Jerusalem. So Jehoshaphat agreed to this alliance, and even confirmed it, saying that the peoples of Judah and Israel are originally one people, and he promised to give him a number of the people and horses equal to the number of people and horses that Israel would send out to war. The army of the kingdom of Judah at that time was large, one million one hundred and sixty thousand. Jehoshaphat erred in his sympathy and his taking part with Ahab in the war, in saying "I am as thou art", for he forgot that Ahab worshiped idols, so how could he unite with one who defies God? This is not sound love, but a concession of the faith and fellowship with the enemies of God. On the other hand, Ahab thought with human logic that Aram was a great power, so he allied with Jehoshaphat to have a larger army, and forgot that victory is from God, and because he was far from God, He did not support him in the war. Perhaps he did not understand that the victory he first achieved over Aram was, as the prophet told him, so that Aram might understand God's power, which is stronger than the pagan gods, and was not because of Ahab's godliness; on the contrary, when Ahab sinned Elijah rebuked him and declared to him God's punishment. He neglected repentance and thought only of relying on human strength; therefore he was defeated in the war and killed, as we shall see in the following verses.

22.4.0.en: Jehoshaphat neglected to ask God before going out with Ahab to war against Aram, but he remembered this after this promise and asked Ahab to inquire of God by means of a prophet, and this shows:

22.4.1.en: 1- Jehoshaphat's godliness and his concern to inquire of God.

22.4.2.en: 2- His entanglement in the alliance with Ahab, because he had become related to him by marriage and made relations of affection with him, although he was wicked, against God, and an idol worshiper. And his going down to Samaria, the place of idol worship, took him away from Jerusalem, where God's temple was, in which he could have inquired through the priests by means of the Urim and Thummim, through which God declares His voice, and they are two stones, one of which had written on it yes and the other no, so one of them lights up to declare the voice of God.

22.4.3.en: Learn to ask God before you enter into any work, and not after you have entered into it and become bound to it and it is hard for you to get out of it, and God may not answer you because of the uprightness of your heart, if you relied on yourself and neglected Him. And know that God loves you, but you too must love Him and want Him, so that He may guide you and keep you from all evil. Put Him before everything and submit to Him, and you will hear His voice.

22.5.0.en: When Ahab heard Jehoshaphat's request, he took refuge with those nearest to him, the prophets of the idols, that is, the false prophets, who were probably the four hundred prophets of Ashtaroth, whom Jezebel sustains. This shows how attached Ahab was to idol worship and his rejection of God, forgetting that his first and second victories over Aram were by God's power and not Baal's, as is clear from the words of God's prophet.

22.5.1.en: And when Ahab asked the four hundred prophets, they thought by human logic that since Ahab had won twice over Aram with a small army, then all the more, when he gathers all his army and allies with Jehoshaphat, he would of course win. So they said to him: be at ease, you will win and recover Ramoth-gilead. In this they forgot that God is the cause of the victory over Aram, as is clear in the words of His prophet.

22.5.2.en: The crookedness of these prophets' words is to be noticed, for they said that the Lord says to you that He will deliver Ramoth-gilead into your hand, and they did not say "the LORD", so that Jehoshaphat would understand that what is meant by "the Lord" is the LORD, and Ahab would understand that what is meant by "the Lord" is Baal. But Jehoshaphat understood that they were false prophets because they did not mention the name of the LORD; and perhaps he noticed the hypocrisy, pretense and flattery in their words.

22.5.3.en: It is understood from the above that the gathering of four hundred on one opinion is not proof of its soundness, for it may be an agreement on evil, as happened here.

22.6.0.en: Since Jehoshaphat realized that these prophets were false, as was mentioned before in (v. 6), he did not believe their words, especially since the words of the wicked do not give peace, and he did not feel at ease. So he asked Ahab about a true prophet of God, to learn from him whether he should enter the war or not.

22.7.0.en: Micaiah the son of Imlah: a prophet of God who appeared in the days of Ahab, and he is different from Micah the writer of the book in the Holy Bible, who appeared about a hundred years after this time.

22.7.1.en: Ahab answered Jehoshaphat that there was a prophet of God, but he did not like him because he always spoke evil about him, and this shows:

22.7.2.en: 1- That God had sent Micaiah to Ahab more than once before to rebuke him for his evil.

22.7.3.en: 2- That Ahab was troubled by Micaiah so that he put him in prison, as appears from (v. 26), when he asked that he be returned to the prison where he had been.

22.7.4.en: 3- That Ahab persisted in evil and in not repenting, for he gathers false prophets who agree with him in his evil and rejects God's word by the mouth of Micaiah.

22.7.5.en: But Jehoshaphat rebuked Ahab for rejecting the word of Micaiah the prophet of God, and in this he shows himself to be a godly man who worships God. But sadly, his mixing with the wicked Ahab made him give up God's guidance, so he entered the war with him, as we shall see, despite God's clear warning by the mouth of Micaiah.

22.7.6.en: Do not refuse to hear the voice of God that comes to you through those around you, if he is reproaching you or rebuking you, but review yourself and repent. And beware of gathering around you a group of hypocrites who falsely make you believe that you are righteous, and others do not frighten you, so that they refrain from declaring the truth to you because you attack, and by this you deprive yourself of hearing the voice of God.

22.8.0.en: Ahab was compelled, to honor his friend Jehoshaphat, to summon Micaiah the prophet quickly, because he was imprisoned and Ahab knew his place, to hear God's voice from his tongue, and he sent a eunuch to bring him. This means that the kings of the children of Israel used eunuchs, like the kings of the nations, and they were probably non-Jews, because the Law did not allow anyone to be made a eunuch.

22.8.1.en: And we notice that Ahab's response to Jehoshaphat's request did not change his heart, because he did not obey the prophet's word, as will appear in the following verses.

22.9.0.en: All these conversations took place between the two kings Ahab and Jehoshaphat while they sat, each on his throne, wearing his royal garments, and these thrones were portable, carried where the king needed them. They were sitting in the large open space of the city of Samaria beside the gate of the city, for it was the custom to set up a large square beside the gate of the city for the people to gather in it for any important matter, and this square was so large that it held the four hundred prophets as well as the people, to decide in it important matters such as whether to enter war or not. This means that this conversation took place before the people and the false prophets, and this shows Jehoshaphat's courage and his holding fast to God. He did not fear to ask for a prophet of God in a city that worshiped Baal. It also shows Ahab's and his people's persistence in idol worship, since none of the leaders of the people or the king's servants objected to Ahab for his refusal to hear the word of the prophet of God.

22.10.0.en: Before the prophet Micaiah arrived, one of the prophets of Baal came forward, called Zedekiah, who was perhaps one of their chiefs, and he was wearing two horns on his head. In ancient wars they used to wear such horns as a sign of strength and in anticipation of victory. Zedekiah said that Ahab would win and push the Arameans, as an animal pushes other animals with its horns and destroys them.

22.10.1.en: And Zedekiah's hypocrisy appears in the following:

22.10.2.en: 1- That he spoke his words in the name of the LORD, as if God had told him this prophecy.

22.10.3.en: 2- He made two horns symbolizing the two kings, to confirm their victory over Aram.

22.10.4.en: 3- Zedekiah imitated God's true prophets, for he made a visual aid of these horns, to make the king and the people believe that this prophecy was from God. The true prophets such as Elisha and Isaiah used visual aids as God commanded them (2 Kgs 13:15, Isa 20:2).

22.11.0.en: Of course all the false prophets agreed with Zedekiah in his false prophecy and cried out, saying to Ahab: go up to Ramoth-gilead, for you will take it and defeat the Arameans.

22.12.0.en: When the eunuch, Ahab's messenger, reached Micaiah to bring him from the prison to the king, he told him that all the prophets had encouraged the king to go to Ramoth-gilead and fight the Arameans, so his victory over them was assured, and he asked him to say the same to the king, so that his words might be for the king's good. This shows:

22.12.1.en: 1- The eunuch's conviction that the agreement of many on one opinion shows that their opinion is sound.

22.12.2.en: 2- That the king's agreement with his purposes is a comfortable thing, so he encourages Micaiah to this for the king's comfort.

22.12.3.en: 3- Perhaps if Micaiah said words agreeing with the king's purposes, he would release him, so the eunuch is giving Micaiah loving advice to be freed from prison.

22.12.4.en: 4- In the eyes of this eunuch and the people in general, good is agreeing with the king and not obeying God.

22.13.0.en: Micaiah swore by the LORD to declare to the eunuch that he stood before the living LORD and that he would say nothing except what the LORD says to him, and this shows:

22.13.1.en: 1- Micaiah's courage and his holding fast to God's word and obeying it.

22.13.2.en: 2- His readiness to bear suffering for the sake of God's word.

22.13.3.en: 3- His not being affected by the words of people such as the eunuch and the king, for the most important thing is the word of God.

22.14.0.en: When Micaiah arrived before Ahab, Ahab asked him, before all who were present, "Shall we go up to Ramoth-gilead to recover it?" Micaiah answered him with clear sarcasm: go up and you will defeat the Arameans and take Ramoth-gilead. By this he meant: since you insist on going up, go up, and since you want to hear that you will win, I tell you that you will win. Micaiah's words were sarcasm that Ahab and all who were present understood; that is, Ahab understood that he had not told him the truth, but that what he said was a repetition of Ahab's wish.

22.15.0.en: Ahab understood that Micaiah was mocking him and not telling him the truth, but agreeing with his opinions and ridiculing him. Ahab may have asked Micaiah before this about other matters and Micaiah mocked him, or he may have asked him in this situation more than once and Micaiah repeated the same words of sarcasm. Therefore Ahab implored him for God's sake to tell him the truth, for Ahab was afraid of the Arameans, so he adjured him in the name of the LORD. Ahab wants to carry out his wish but at the same time is afraid, so he begged Micaiah to tell him God's word.

22.16.0.en: When Ahab declared his readiness and concern to hear God's word, Micaiah began to declare the prophecy that God had shown him. He said: I saw a vision in which God's people were scattered and spread on the mountains without a shepherd, that is, without a leader, because the leader, who is Ahab, would have been killed in the war, and God said, "let them return every man to his house in peace". For Ben-hadad king of Aram, as we shall see in the coming verses, had as his aim the killing of Ahab, and when he achieved that he stopped the war, so God's people returned in peace.

22.16.2.en: 1- The killing of Ahab in the war.

22.16.3.en: 2- The scattering of the people on the mountains, without leadership.

22.16.4.en: The meaning of this prophecy is clear, which is that they should not enter the war, because Ahab would die and the people would not achieve victory, but God would have compassion on them and bring them back in peace, and perhaps this was for the sake of Jehoshaphat's righteousness. Sadly, Ahab did not benefit from this prophecy and did not obey God, so he died in the war. Likewise Jehoshaphat felt embarrassed to withdraw from the war, so he went out with him and did not obey God's word, which he had sought with concern; but after he heard Micaiah he neglected his word.

22.16.5.en: When God declares His voice to you, whether through your father of confession, or in the Holy Bible, or by the mouth of those around you, or in any way, do not neglect it, because your judgment will become greater and you will meet a dark future, as Ahab did not obey and died with his sin upon him.

22.17.0.en: Ahab was angry when he heard the word of Micaiah the prophet and considered it ill feeling from Micaiah toward him, and refused to accept his words as a prophecy from God. Perhaps he was influenced by the four hundred prophets who encouraged him to go to war. On the other hand, Ahab bore hatred toward God and His prophets, so he thought that they hated him, although the hatred was in his heart to begin with.

22.17.1.en: Here Jehoshaphat's weakness appears, that he was influenced by Ahab's words and did not answer him and call him to obey God, so that in the end he rejected God's word and entered the war with him.

22.18.0.en: Micaiah did not care to defend himself against Ahab's accusation that he speaks evil about him, because Micaiah was occupied with declaring the voice of God.

22.18.1.en: So Micaiah completed the second part of the vision he had seen, for he saw the LORD sitting on His throne in heaven with His angels around Him on the right and on the left. This produced in his heart:

22.18.2.en: 1- Reverence and joy at being in the presence of God.

22.18.3.en: 2- Not being disturbed by Ahab's anger, or the prison into which Ahab had thrown him.

22.18.4.en: 3- His trust in God's word that he declares, and in the falsehood of its opponents from among the prophets of Baal.

22.18.5.en: 4- His faith that everything is in God's hand, so He allows victories, or defeat, or leaves the wicked to fall into their sins.

22.18.6.en: 5- God is the Controller of all; perhaps what is meant by the angels on the right is the angels appointed by God to convey His blessings to mankind, and those on the left are the angels appointed to discipline sinners.

22.19.0.en: The vision that God showed Micaiah was in the form of a dialogue, so that he might understand the reality of the matters and declare them in a way understandable to human beings, although in heaven the matter does not need all these dialogues, for the movement of thought takes place in less than a moment and God declares His command at once.

22.19.1.en: God showed in the vision that He asks before His angels: who can incite Ahab to evil and to disobeying God? Of course God does not want any human being to walk in evil, but He allows Satan to tempt all in the proper measure, and sometimes gives up the wicked if they persist in sin, that perhaps they, and those around them, may feel the seriousness of sin, so that they turn back from it. In Ahab's case, he persisted in rejecting God, so He gave him up, to be an example of evil before his people, that they might repent. When God asked, His angels replied with different opinions or suggestions according to their understanding. All this, as we mentioned, is so that Ahab and the people may understand what is taking place in heaven.

22.20.0.en: Then God allowed Satan, that is, the evil spirit, to stand before Him, and Satan declared that he was able to seduce Ahab. God asked him how he would seduce him. Satan said that he would enter the prophets of Baal and speak lying words through their tongues to deceive Ahab. God said to him that you are indeed able to do so, for Satan is full of evil and wicked tricks, and God allowed him to go out and seduce Ahab because Ahab had sold himself and surrendered to evil.

22.20.1.en: This vision reminds us of what happened at the beginning of the book of Job, for all these are portrayals by God of what takes place in heaven, that we may understand God's righteousness and Satan's evil. By this God gave Ahab a last warning, that he might know that Satan, or the Baal whom he worships, will lead him and his prophets to destruction, that perhaps he might take notice and repent, for God seeks the salvation of all, however great their evil.

22.21.0.en: Micaiah summed up God's voice in the vision for Ahab in two things:

22.21.1.en: 1- That the words of the prophets of Baal are all falsehood.

22.21.2.en: 2- God allowed the evil that befell Ahab, that is, his destruction in the war. And this is the end of the most wicked of the kings of Israel.

22.22.s.en: (4) The striking and imprisonment of Micaiah

22.22.0.en: With insolence and wickedness Zedekiah, who was probably the chief of the prophets of Baal, came forward and struck Micaiah on the cheek, and did not ask Ahab's permission for it, but he knew well that Ahab supported his prophets, that is, the prophets of Baal. As for Jehoshaphat, as a guest with no authority, he did nothing, although in truth he could at least have declared that this was wrong, but he was weak and slack, despite his confidence that Micaiah was the true prophet and all the other prophets were false, and Jehoshaphat, as a believer in God, is able to distinguish the true prophet from the false.

22.22.1.en: Then Zedekiah said to Micaiah in astonishment and mockery: how did you dare, Micaiah, and claim that the Spirit of God who is upon me has passed by and come to you?

22.22.3.en: 1- The boldness of evil and its assault on the children of God.

22.22.4.en: 2- The lie and sophistry by which Satan, through his children, tries to deceive people, for although Micaiah is the true prophet and Zedekiah and those with him are all liars, the lying Zedekiah claims that the Spirit of God is with him only and not with Micaiah. Of course the Spirit of God does not harm others, as Zedekiah struck Micaiah, for the Spirit of God is gentle and firm but not violent and harsh.

22.23.0.en: Micaiah bore the blow for God's sake and did not defend himself, but was occupied with confirming God's voice to Zedekiah. He said to him: you will understand and know God's word when it comes to pass and God's people are defeated before Aram and flee from it, and you, Zedekiah, will flee from house to house and from room to room, either for fear of the Arameans or of Jezebel, who will be disturbed by the death of her husband and will try to kill Zedekiah, who lied and led her husband astray, so that he died.

22.23.1.en: Let your aim be to declare the voice of God even if the wicked rise against you and insult you. Bear it for God's sake, confident that God appreciates your labor and will support you, and prepares for you a great crown in heaven.

22.24.0.en: In anger and pride Ahab commanded the eunuch who had brought Micaiah to return him to the prison under the authority and responsibility of Amon, the governor of the city of Samaria, and Joash, Ahab's son, who apparently was in charge of the prison.

22.24.1.en: And in going further in his pride Ahab commanded that they afflict Micaiah in the prison, giving him only the barest amount of water and the worst food, to humiliate him because of the lie he had told and the evil words he had spoken against Ahab. So Ahab believed, and added that they should do this until Ahab returns in peace. This shows that evil blinds the eyes of its owner, so that he does not see the truth, however clear.

22.25.0.en: Micaiah was not disturbed by Ahab's arbitrary orders of imprisonment and ill treatment within it, but continued to confirm God's voice before all the people, declaring to Ahab that he would surely not return from the war, because he would die, and if he returned, then God had not spoken. For Micaiah was sure of God's vision and commands, and declared them to all the people, so that when they see Ahab killed they will repent and return to God.

22.26.s.en: (5) The war against Aram and the death of Ahab

22.26.0.en: Despite all of God's clear declarations by the mouth of Micaiah that they should not enter, Ahab went up with his army, and with him Jehoshaphat with the army of Judah, to Ramoth-gilead to recover it from the Arameans. While Ahab persisted in harm because of his distance from God, Jehoshaphat's position is the strange one, in entering the war despite all these warnings, and this appears to be for the following reasons:

22.26.1.en: 1- Jehoshaphat's previous promise to Ahab to go with him to the war, and kings do not go back on their word; but of course it is possible to go back if God has commanded the opposite of the king's word.

22.26.2.en: 2- Jehoshaphat's weakness before his relative by marriage Ahab, for he found himself embarrassed to leave him alone, because Ahab insisted on entering the war, completely despising God's word.

22.26.3.en: 3- Perhaps he understood that only Ahab would die, but he and all the people would return in peace, as Micaiah said, so he took courage and went with Ahab. But this is a great mistake, since in it there is opposition to God's word, and he did not heed Micaiah's word.

22.26.4.en: 4- Jehoshaphat's doubt of God's word through Micaiah, and what may have helped him in this was Ahab's anger and his and his prophets' accusation of Micaiah that he speaks evil. And this is a natural result of mixing with the wicked, that a person goes astray and his faith in God weakens.

22.27.0.en: Ahab felt that he was the target of Ben-hadad in this war, especially after hearing Micaiah's prophecy of his death, so he was even more afraid and decided to enter the war in disguise, as an ordinary soldier. But can he disguise himself before God? Since God had decided that he would be killed, there was no solution except that he repent and believe in God, and He would have mercy on him. Perhaps Ahab's disguise came from what he had heard from Micaiah, that God's people would be scattered on the mountains, so he decided to disguise himself so as not to be killed and to remain leader of his people, so that they would not be defeated or scattered. By this he is trying to stop God's judgment, which, as we said, cannot be stopped except by repentance.

22.27.1.en: Ahab announced to Jehoshaphat that he would disguise himself, but proposed to Jehoshaphat that he put on his royal garments, and this was a great evil from Ahab, to expose his friend, who had come to ally with him, to die in the war in his place. Ahab disguised himself, while Jehoshaphat put on the royal garments, although it was unwise of Jehoshaphat to agree to this. Why, then, did Jehoshaphat agree?

22.27.2.en: 1- Perhaps he felt pride in being the sole commander of the armies in his royal garments.

22.27.3.en: 2- His trust in God's word by the mouth of Micaiah, that the one who would die was Ahab, because God had spoken evil about him, and Micaiah had not directed a rebuke or divine judgment to Jehoshaphat.

22.28.0.en: Ben-hadad king of Aram organized his army, made up of thirty-two divisions, each led by a commander who was one of the vassal kings, who are the heads of the provinces mentioned in (ch. 20:1). He commanded these commanders to concentrate on killing Ahab, in order to reduce the number of the dead in his army, because he knew that if the commander of the army of Israel, who was Ahab, were killed, the army would scatter at once and the victory would be Aram's.

22.29.0.en: The captains of the chariots searched for the king of Israel, and saw from afar a person wearing the royal garments, and they thought he was Ahab and attacked him. Here Jehoshaphat cried out at once and they left him, and this cry means the following:

22.29.1.en: 1- A cry to God to save him from death, and this shows his faith in the hour of danger, so God drew the soldiers of Aram away from him, as appears in (2 Chr 18:31).

22.29.2.en: 2- He cried out declaring before the soldiers that he was not Ahab, so they left him, with God's help, for God made them leave him to search for Ahab, as Ben-hadad had commanded them. Perhaps some of them knew Ahab's appearance and voice from the former wars, since they accompanied Ben-hadad during the treaty that Ahab made with him (ch. 20:31-34).

22.29.3.en: 3- Because Jehoshaphat believed Micaiah's prophecy that the one who would meet evil was Ahab (v. 23,), he hurried to declare to the Aramean soldiers that he was not Ahab, so that they would leave him.

22.29.4.en: Jehoshaphat was exposed to death, and God allowed this because of the mistakes he made, which are:

22.29.5.en: 1- His mixing with the wicked, even becoming related to them by marriage, that is, mixing with Ahab and the marriage of his son to Ahab's daughter.

22.29.6.en: 2- His not obeying God's word by the mouth of Micaiah, which was clear, not to enter the war, because its result was defeat.

22.29.7.en: 3- His love of leadership and of appearing as commander of all the armies of God's people; but God saved him from death because of his faith in Him and his return to Him in the hour of danger.

22.30.0.en: Drew a bow: he pulled his bow back, so the arrow that was in the bow was released.

22.30.1.en: The joints of the harness: the area between the armor that protects the chest and the armor that protects the thighs, and the two pieces of armor are joined by linen connections, so it is the region of the belly.

22.30.2.en: Turn thine hand: stop the chariot's moving forward and turn the chariot to go in the opposite direction, that is, to leave the battle.

22.30.3.en: An Aramean soldier was holding his bow with an arrow in it, and perhaps he was trying to fix it, or test it, so the arrow was released without intent, and struck the disguised Ahab in the belly with a deep wound whose seriousness Ahab felt, so he asked the driver of his chariot to turn the chariot and take him out of the battle.

22.30.4.en: We notice that the disguised Ahab was struck by a stray arrow with a deep wound that killed him, while Jehoshaphat, who wore the royal garments, was protected by God from death because he cried out to Him. For God's judgment must be carried out, however much the wicked man tries to protect himself, and the righteous save themselves by faith and prayer.

22.30.5.en: God allowed Ahab to die and not be taken by Ben-hadad alive, because he might pardon him in return for Ahab's earlier kindness; for God's judgment was Ahab's destruction because of his many evils.

22.30.6.en: You cannot escape from the hand of God, so do not commit sin in secret, because He sees you, and the wages of sin is death, and the only solution is to return to God by repentance, for He is a tender Father ready to forgive you everything, and the Church always opens her arms with forgiveness in the sacraments of confession and Communion.

22.31.0.en: The driver of the king's chariot and the commanders around his chariot did not approve of Ahab leaving the battle, lest his army scatter if they learned that he had been seriously wounded. So they supported him and kept him standing in his chariot, although his blood was flowing abundantly and ran onto the floor of the chariot, and even one who noticed his wound would think it a slight one. The fighting continued fiercely with the Arameans until evening, when King Ahab died.

22.32.0.en: The news spread quickly among the soldiers of Israel that their king Ahab had died, so their commanders called for withdrawal and for every soldier to return to his home, whether the soldiers of Israel or of Judah, for the following reasons:

22.32.1.en: 1- The death of the commander leaves the army without leadership, so it is impossible to continue the war, and this shows the importance of the commander, especially in ancient times.

22.32.2.en: 2- Perhaps some of them remembered Micaiah's prophecy that Ahab would die and the soldiers would be spread on the mountains, fleeing and scattered, so they hurried to withdraw.

22.32.3.en: 3- The Arameans heard of Ahab's death and saw the army's withdrawal, so they stopped the fighting and withdrew too, since their aim was to kill Ahab and thereby keep Ramoth-gilead subject to them. So the Arameans withdrew also, and thus the war lasted only one day and ended.

22.33.0.en: The soldiers of Israel returned with their dead king to Samaria, his capital, which his father Omri had built, and buried him there.

22.34.0.en: Here details are explained about the transport of the dead Ahab and his chariot and how his blood was washed. They passed through the city of Jezreel on their way to Samaria; there they washed his chariot and weapons in a pool outside Jezreel, called the pool of Samaria, then they carried him to Samaria. By this the word of Elijah the prophet to Ahab was fulfilled after his killing of Naboth the Jezreelite and seizing his field: the dogs licked the blood of Naboth, since Elijah said that the dogs would lick your blood, Ahab, in the same place where they licked the blood of the wronged Naboth (ch. 21:19). There is another opinion, that the soldiers washed the chariot in the pool of Samaria, which lies beside the city of Samaria, and the dogs licked Ahab's blood there, as the dogs licked Naboth's blood outside Jezreel, but the first opinion is the more likely.

22.34.1.en: The place where Ahab's chariot was washed, in the pool of Samaria, is the place where the harlots who were dedicated to harlotry in the temples of Baal, which Ahab encouraged, used to wash; that is, in the end Ahab's blood was washed in an unclean place, because he defiled himself by the worship of Baal throughout his life, and so he died a shameful, unclean death.

22.34.2.en: And so the great royal chariot was washed for another king to use, and Ahab died and took nothing, as all die; and if he had remembered that, he would have repented and returned to God.

22.35.0.en: Ahab was concerned with building palaces and cities, especially a great house that he adorned with ivory, which is taken from the tusks of elephants, and it was called the ivory house. So all his concern was material, far from spiritual things. All these matters and the account of his death are mentioned in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel, which is different from the Book of Chronicles in the Holy Bible. And after his death his son Ahaziah reigned in his place.

22.36.s.en: (6) Jehoshaphat king of Judah and his most important works

22.36.0.en: In the fourth year of Ahab's reign over Israel, Jehoshaphat the son of Asa began to reign over the kingdom of Judah, and he was at that time thirty-five years old, and he reigned twenty-five years over Judah. Jehoshaphat's mother was called Azubah the daughter of Shilhi, and it seems that she was a godly person, for her husband Asa was righteous and did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, and likewise her son Jehoshaphat walked like his father with uprightness of heart. The Holy Bible mentions some mothers to show their holy role, or on the contrary the evil one, which appears in husbands and sons, like the wicked Jezebel, the wife of Ahab and the mother of Ahaziah and Athaliah, all of whom were wicked. The details of the life and works of Jehoshaphat are mentioned in (2 Chr 17-20).

22.37.0.en: The Holy Bible gives us a summary of the life of Jehoshaphat and his most important works.

22.37.1.en: If Asa was upright in the eyes of the LORD, indeed perfect (ch. 15:14), then Jehoshaphat his son walked in the upright way of his father before God, that is, he cared for the worship of God in His temple and rejected idol worship in all its forms.

22.37.2.en: The offering of sacrifices on the high places and the burning of incense was personal worship, while public worship remained in the temple.

22.37.3.en: But the mistake that Jehoshaphat did not correct was that he allowed sacrificing on the high places to God and not to the idols, although God commanded that the offering of sacrifices be in His temple only and forbade that it be on the high places (Deut 12:13, 14), because these high places turned in time into idol worship.

22.38.0.en: The greatest mistake Jehoshaphat fell into was his reconciliation, alliance and association with the king of Israel, who was wicked, Ahab, and then his son Ahaziah. Although understanding and reconciliation between neighboring states is useful, in addition to the fact that the kingdoms of Israel and Judah are originally one nation, God's people, yet on the other hand alliance with the wicked has many harms, and this is what Jehoshaphat fell into. The reconciliation and alliance appeared in the following:

22.38.1.en: 1- His alliance with Ahab in the war against Aram to recover Ramoth-gilead (v. 32).

22.38.2.en: 2- The marrying of his son Joram to Athaliah the daughter of Ahab.

22.38.3.en: 3- His going out to war with Ahaziah the son of Ahab against Moab (2 Kgs 3:7).

22.38.4.en: 4- His partnership with Ahaziah in building a fleet of trading ships (2 Chr 20:36). This reconciliation with the kings of Israel brought many troubles on Jehoshaphat, because of the LORD's anger with him. The most important of these troubles:-

22.38.5.en: 1- His exposure to death in his war with Ahab against Aram, and God saved him at the last moment (v. 32).

22.38.6.en: 2- His causing his son Joram to stumble by marrying him to Athaliah, who introduced the worship of Baal into Judah and dominated the kingdom, for she killed her grandchildren and sat on the throne of Judah (2 Kgs 11:1).

22.38.7.en: 3- The breaking of the trading fleet at Ezion-geber, and Jehoshaphat lost much, because he angered the LORD, and God declared this to him by Eliezer the prophet (2 Chr 20:37). It is noticed that Jehoshaphat did not quickly learn the danger of mixing with the wicked, for what befell him from his mixing with Ahab did not make him keep away from Ahaziah, his wicked son; therefore God was angry with him and his ships were broken, but finally he learned obedience to God, so he refused Ahaziah's offer to share in the trade by ships (v. 49). But the love of Christ, the Redeemer of sinners, appears in that He came from the descendants of Joram the son of Jehoshaphat and Athaliah his wife (Mt 1:8, 9), for He seeks the salvation of everyone who believed and tried to obey God, like Jehoshaphat.

22.38.8.en: It is good to be at peace with all, as far as you can, but beware of mixing with the wicked, or sharing in their works by your own choice, lest you be defiled by their thoughts and behavior, and so anger the LORD and He abandons you. Let your heart be open with love toward all, but be careful about whom you choose as friends and those close to you.

22.39.0.en: Jehoshaphat was strong in facing idol worship, so he removed it and all the corruption connected with it. On the other hand, his superiority in wars against the surrounding nations appeared, such as the Ammonites and the Moabites (2 Chr 20:1). The details of Jehoshaphat's works are written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah, which is a historical book concerning the kings of Judah, and is different from the Book of Chronicles in the Holy Bible.

22.40.0.en: The sodomites: the men who gave themselves to the pagan gods, to practice homosexual acts with them, and who live in houses beside the temples so that males may lie with them, and by this they please the gods according to their belief.

22.40.1.en: Asa destroyed idol worship and all the adultery and perversion connected with it, but it seems that some sodomites were able to flee and continued their sexual practice, so Jehoshaphat completed what his father Asa had done and destroyed the remainder of these sodomites, that is, he removed the corruption from the land, so as not to put a stumbling block before his people, that they might worship the LORD in purity.

22.41.0.en: The kingdom of Edom lived in the mountains of Seir and extended south and east of the kingdom of Judah, from the Dead Sea to the Gulf of Aqaba. Edom was subjected to many attacks from the kings of the children of Israel, among them Saul (1 Sam 14:47), then David, who destroyed all the males. Edom grew strong in part in the days of Solomon, and it seems that it was weak in the days of Jehoshaphat, so he set over it a deputy from himself, that is, a representative of Jehoshaphat, and he may have been from the Edomites themselves; that is, Edom was under the control of Judah.

22.42.0.en: Tarshish: a famous trading city in the south of Spain on the Mediterranean coast. Gold and many goods were imported from it.

22.42.1.en: Ophir: a city lying in the south of the Arabian Peninsula in the present state of Yemen, famous for producing the purest kinds of gold (Sir 7:20), and it was named Ophir after one of the descendants of Shem (Gen 10:29). Ezion-geber: a famous ancient port on the Gulf of Aqaba, lying west of the present city of Eilat. Jehoshaphat built huge trading ships able to go to the farthest country known at that time, which was Tarshish, lying at the end of the Mediterranean Sea, the end of the ancient world, in order to send them to Tarshish, joining in this with Ahaziah king of Israel, but the ships were broken, because of God's anger with Jehoshaphat for his partnership with the wicked, that is, Ahaziah (2 Chr 20:37). Then Jehoshaphat built other strong ships like the first, and Ahaziah asked him to join him in the trade, but Jehoshaphat refused, for he had finally learned to obey God and not to share in work with the wicked.

22.43.0.en: After twenty-five years of reign, Jehoshaphat, the righteous king, finally died. And his firstborn son Jehoram reigned after him (2 Chr 21:3), and sadly he was not righteous like his father, because of his marriage to the wicked Athaliah the daughter of Ahab, and this shows the importance of choosing a righteous wife.

22.44.0.en: After the death of Ahab in the battle of Ramoth-gilead, his son Ahaziah reigned over the kingdom of Israel, and because of his evils and his worship of idols the LORD allowed illnesses upon him and he died quickly, so he reigned only two years in his capital Samaria.

22.45.0.en: The details of Ahaziah's evils are that he continued in the worship of the golden calves that Jeroboam the son of Nebat set up in Bethel and Dan, and also continued in the worship of the idols that his father and mother introduced, such as Baal and Ashtaroth. By this he defied God and provoked Him by his persistence in idol worship, because he not only allowed it, but himself led the people in bowing down to the idols and worshiping them. And he did not learn from the danger of disobeying God in the days of his father, who did not obey Elijah, who withheld the rain and brought down fire from heaven and killed the prophets of Baal, and yet Ahab did not return to God, and he did not obey Micaiah either, who warned Ahab not to enter the war with Aram, but he obeyed the false prophets and died.

22.45.1.en: Be careful in all your actions, whether you are a father, or a leader, or responsible anywhere; indeed, since you are a Christian you are the light of the world, so do not be lax in your words or actions, lest you cause others to stumble. You are the image of God, even if all around you are wicked.

22.45.2.en: We see that this book began with the greatest of the kings of the children of Israel, David, when the kingdom was united, and ends with the most wicked of the kings of the kingdom of Israel, Ahab, after the division of the kingdom. Why did it begin with a joyful beginning and end with a shameful end? The reason is clear: the relation between the king and the people was strong in the days of David, but at the end of the book we find how they left God and worshiped idols and walked in many evils and uncleanness, so they were defeated before their enemies the Arameans, and Ahab died, as a punishment for his evils, a shameful death in the war.

22.45.3.en: A comparison between the false prophets and the prophets of God; serial; the false prophets; the prophets of God

22.45.4.en: 1- They speak false messages of their own composition and not true messages, because they do not speak from God. Except what God says to them.

22.45.5.en: 2- They have personal purposes. They speak God's word even if it exposes them to many troubles, as the prophet who spoke against the altar before Jeroboam was exposed to death, but God rescued him when Jeroboam's hand dried up (ch. 13:4).

22.45.6.en: 3- They hold political positions because they please rejected by the wicked kings and do not seek the kings. to the positions.

22.45.7.en: 4- Rich, they care about their material gains. Poor, detached, they live for God and are content with food and clothing.

22.45.8.en: 5- The kings love them because they agree with them, but they are merely, even if one prophet before the followers of the kings, and the kings rely on the multitude of many, like Elijah, who stands before four hundred in number, since they have no awe. of the prophets of Baal and four hundred and fifty of the prophets of the groves (ch. 18:19)

22.45.9.en: 6- They try to flatter the kings and the people, so they say what pleases them, and they rely on their minds in; and the people as a rebuke; or divine punishment for them, such as deducing the future (ch. 22:5-12); they speak God's word even if it troubles the kings. The prophet's word to Ahab that he would die instead of Ben-hadad king of Aram, whom he released (ch. 20:42)
